insights.quote: That's unfortunately after more than 20 years in academia, the thing that I can recommend the most based on scientific literature, not on storytelling, that's something different based on scientific literature. Yeah, as a private investor, try to have a mid or long term perspective of 10, 15, 20 years and go well diversified, broadly diversified in different index products and do not trade much because this will always harm your net performance, the trading costs. They are evil.
insights.summary: Passive, long-term investing in diversified index funds outperforms active trading due to transaction costs and behavioral biases.
insights.speaker: Michael Kirchler

insights.quote: Index funds, here we go. Yeah, exactly. So, Michael, I have another question here. The energy market. Sorry, D? The energy market. Oh, yes. Yes, I like specifics. Would you see that there's a tendency for maybe bubble form formation there? I mean, in terms of, I mean, it's just the demand and we'll call it supply. Yeah, demand and supply. And basically supply being very limited right now and the demand being equal to what it used to be or kind of even higher. It's a very interesting and highly relevant market at the moment because a lot of people suffer because of this high energy prices. And I think they will even suffer more during next winter.
insights.summary: Energy price increases are driven by fundamental supply-demand imbalances rather than speculative bubbles.
insights.speaker: Michael Kirchler

insights.quote: I mean, 1.5 percent doesn't sound that much per year, but it's around a quarter of what you can expect in return or in performance every year, and that's insane. And this makes you basically dead after 20 or 30 years, because then you have, I think, your final portfolio value after 30 years will probably be around 40 or 50 percent of what you would have without management fee.
insights.summary: Management fees compound over time and can reduce final portfolio value by 40-50% over 30 years.
insights.speaker: Markus Gedda

insights.quote: To protect yourself from it, you could say you could give yourself targets where you say, okay, if I already made 50 or 60 percent, I will go out of the asset. But then you should no longer look how the assets are developed in the future, because you will never have the right position where you go out and you will always be fed up that you didn't find the perfect timing.
insights.summary: Set profit targets and avoid looking back to prevent regret and psychological trap of trying to find perfect timing.
insights.speaker: Michael Kirchler

insights.quote: I think confirmation bias, I think, is really extremely bad, and all of us should be very aware about it. Another bias is, or another behavioral pattern, I would say, that is interesting, that I tried to avoid is probability weighting bias. That's our tendency that we overweight low probabilities and we underweight high probabilities.
insights.summary: Confirmation bias leads investors to seek information that supports existing beliefs, while probability weighting causes overestimation of low-probability events like lottery stocks.
insights.speaker: Michael Kirchler

insights.quote: I think that there are two perspectives on that. Sorry, that's an answer of a professor. One perspective is, for me, as an individual investor, what do I learn or how do I spot potential bubbles and how do I trade? And the other perspective is from a societal perspective or the perspective of the regulator, how to spot the bubble and maybe try to prevent the bubble. Here my answer is, there will always be bubbles in the future as well, and there have always been some. And it's pretty difficult to prevent future bubbles. That's... I'm sorry, I have no better news here.
insights.summary: Bubbles are inevitable in markets and difficult to identify in real-time; focus on protecting yourself rather than predicting them.
insights.speaker: Michael Kirchler

insights.quote: So this is one of the historical reasons why bubbles emerge. So simply demand pressure and therefore prices are built up pretty strongly. And this was one of the reasons for the dot-com bubble that a herd of inexperienced traders all of a sudden entered the market. And studies also show that smart money left the market earlier than the private investors left.
insights.summary: Bubbles often emerge when inexperienced investors herd into markets, while institutional investors exit earlier.
insights.speaker: Michael Kirchler

insights.quote: Loss aversion means if you for instance want to purchase a car or a new bicycle or any other equipment that is more expensive, usually you get trial offers. You can try the car for one or two days or maybe three months on Netflix. And then you already feel like you have this product and you feel how great the car is and the gym membership is good and Netflix is great and so on. And then losing it or giving it away, so not buying the car or not prolonging the gym membership or Netflix membership would be like a loss in that perspective.
insights.summary: Trial offers exploit loss aversion - once you experience a product, the psychological pain of losing it makes you more likely to purchase.
insights.speaker: Michael Kirchler

crypto_mentions.speaker: Michael Kirchler

crypto_mentions.context: Example of herding behavior by private investors in bubbles

summary: This episode features Professor Michael Kirchler discussing behavioral finance, human biases in investing, and market psychology. The conversation covers anchoring effects, framing bias, loss aversion, and confirmation bias. The professor provides research-based investment advice favoring passive, long-term index fund investing over active trading. Discussion also touches on market bubbles, the current energy market situation, and how behavioral patterns affect individual investors during market downturns.
key_takeaways: Passive, long-term index fund investing with minimal trading outperforms active strategies due to transaction costs and behavioral biases
Management fees of 1.5-2% can reduce final portfolio value by 40-50% over 30 years through compounding
Bubbles are driven by herding of inexperienced investors, while smart money exits earlier
Key behavioral biases to watch: confirmation bias, loss aversion, probability weighting, anchoring, and framing effect
Energy price increases are driven by fundamental supply-demand issues rather than speculative bubbles
